searchText: <@486501030046203915> Hmm, good point. I don't think it clicked with me previously that if the base fee is sufficiently high you'll eat into the miner bribe. That is a pretty strong argument for the current parameter set and naming. I will let this knowledge percolate for a bit and see how I feel after it has sunk in. Where are current implementations putting the base fee in the block header? At the end (after the nonce)? I found an inconsistency in the specification, curious how implementers have implemented it. At the fork block, do you set the EIP-1559 gas **limit** to half of the block size, or do you set the EIP-1559 gas **target** to half of the block size? I'm pretty sure **target** is correct, otherwise we run into a problem where large transactions can't be included in Ethereum for 800,000 blocks and I think the other formulas in the spec don't make sense if you use **limit**. It appears there is another issue where the spec suggests that the base fee delta for block `n` (relative to block `n-1`) is calculated by looking at the fullness of block `n`. I believe it should be that base fee delta for block `n` is calculated by looking at the fullness of block `n-1`. That is, a miner doesn't have control over the base fee for the block they are producing, they only have control over the base fee for the following block. As I'm trying to clean up this spec while retaining its general style, I'm reminded of this commit which echoes my feelings about having a special specification syntax: Maybe one day someone can explain to me why we write EIPs in pseudocode instead of actual code. Every time I do it I struggle compared to if I just wrote a tiny little go/rust/typescript/c#/python library (e.g., a function or two). > Maybe one day someone can explain to me why we write EIPs in pseudocode instead of actual code. Every time I do it I struggle compared to if I just wrote a tiny little go/rust/typescript/c#/python library (e.g., a function or two). <@!301186049323958275> They should be written in python. I'm not sure why they aren't. I'm actually writing up EIP-1559 in python right now, maybe I'll submit a PR that just swaps out the spec with Python (which means the tests can also run against the spec itself, which is a nice bonus). Do transactions have the `gas_limit * gas_price` deducted from their account first, then the transaction executed, then `gas_refund * gas_price` refunded to their account? Ah, I suppose it doesn't really matter since at the moment the only way to move a user's ETH is by setting the `value` on the transaction, which is part of the transaction. What is the rationale for allowing miners to cover `base_fee` for transactions? It feels like it adds a tad bit of complexity, and I don't really see a clear benefit. > It appears there is another issue where the spec suggests that the base fee delta for block `n` (relative to block `n-1`) is calculated by looking at the fullness of block `n`. I believe it should be that base fee delta for block `n` is calculated by looking at the fullness of block `n-1`. <@!301186049323958275> I agree that this is how the spec is written, but I also find it more natural to have transactions in block `n` experience basefee after block `n-1`. trying to think of arguments against <@!486501030046203915> Do you know how things are currently implemented? yeah, the basefee of block n definitely "should" depend only on things that happen before block n I'm pretty sure using block `n`'s fullness to calculate `base_fee` for the block is incorrect (just a mistake in the spec). I'm not even sure how you would build a block like that since you don't know how much gas money to deduct from the signer before fully executing the block, and you need to know that to know whether a transaction is valid *before* you include it in a block. If the `fee_cap` and `gas_premium` are both `0` and a miner includes the transaction, does that mean the signer account doesn't need to have any balance to execute the transaction, since the miner is paying for gas? ~~Means we need another conditional to avoid giving the signer a flash loan for the duration of the transaction. 😢~~ Hmm, maybe not. I think it naturally stays positive. > <@!486501030046203915> Do you know how things are currently implemented? <@!301186049323958275> I don't know go but from a quick search for places where basefee is set in the vulcanize repo I think it is implemented as we think it should be, and not as the specs define it I'm going to move forward assuming it was just a bug in the spec and everyone implemented it "correctly". I feel like someone would have complained during implementation if not. 🙂 I also kind of dislike how a miner with a buggy transaction inclusion algorithm can end up draining their own account. specifically this line: https://github.com/vulcanize/go-ethereum/blob/eip1559_rebase/consensus/misc/basefee.go#L78 it's also how i implemented the simulations (btw a new one is here: https://twitter.com/barnabemonnot/status/1289243605358452738) > What is the rationale for allowing miners to cover `base_fee` for transactions? It feels like it adds a tad bit of complexity, and I don't really see a clear benefit. <@!301186049323958275> can't find a source but I remember it as miners can use it to include invalid transactions they like, in which case they have to subsidise the missing basefee <@!486501030046203915> Any idea what the use case for that is? In theory, it enables miner-sponsored transactions, but I feel like EIP-2711 is a much better and more generalized solution to that particular problem (sponsored transactions), and since it *likely* will get added anyway (potentially at same time or earlier than 1559) we shouldn't try to use 1559 to solve sponsored transactions. not familiar with 2711 but yes that seems to address this use case has been it been considered to also burn a % of tips to miners ? Hey <@!574864862338088960> gonna look into the testnet a bit today
